usedLessons.text: Top lesson: BLG's win backed my belief that stronger individual players win series, but I got there partly by leaning on the region gap, and that gap only counts when the scouting report flags it as big. Next time I'll start from the lane matchups (who can take a lane and hold it, as Viper, Bin and Knight did) and check the region flag separately, without quoting percentages unless the report calls the gap big. (from Swiss BLG vs KC; picked BLG, actual BLG 1-0)

Top lesson: Player skill won this series, so keep anchoring on the lane-by-lane gaps (Viper and Knight over their counterparts) and stop pointing at the crowd as if its mood proves or disproves anything. Top lesson: Individual skill still wins series, but I have to compare players lane by lane. Distrusting the crowd only works when the crowd is wrong about who has the stronger players, and this time the hype and the better roster pointed to the same team. Top lesson: Individual skill still wins series, but I have to judge it by who is actually winning their matchup now, and Knight beating Zeka in mid showed that a past final win and a "best pair" label don't settle a lane. usedLessons.text: Jungle lesson: When the early-game tempo data (first blood, first tower, Herald and dragon control) points at one side, don't let region labels or an old series result talk me out of it. And if the way I'd be wrong is already showing up in the stats, as BLG's early leads were, I should take that as the pick, not as a footnote. (from Swiss HLE vs BLG; picked HLE 2-1, actual BLG 2-0)

Jungle lesson: The early map is still what decides games, but my flip trigger worked best because it was specific (KC taking the first Herald and first dragon off a jungle skirmish), so I should keep naming a concrete early-tempo trigger like that in every call. A big region gap still sets my baseline, but if the underdog's early game is clearly cleaner, I'll stop assuming the favorite's lead will hold and lean toward the sweep.
